This vignette walks through the ST1 example: 25 human samples stained
with a 31-channel T cell panel on a BD instrument, gated with the ST1 gate
hierarchy (52 population gates and 363 activation gates). The ST1 inputs are
in `scripts/ST1` of the source repository; the FCS files are not distributed
with the package, so the code is not run here.

## The idea

Manual gating draws the same gates on every sample by eye. AutoGating
describes each gate by *how* it should be placed rather than *where*: "the
threshold on CD4 where the negative and positive populations cross", "the
band of events where FSC-H follows FSC-A". The gates are first calculated on
pooled events from a set of training samples, giving a model; the model is
then applied to every sample, either at the trained positions ("fixed") or
calculated again on each sample ("recalculate") with a warning when a gate
moves further than expected.

Models are Honeychrome `.agmodel` files, so a model built in R opens in
Honeychrome's Automated Gating plugin, and a model built in Honeychrome runs
here.

## Inputs

Three files describe an experiment.

The **panel** (`fcs_panel_st1.csv`) lists each channel to read: its FCS name
(`dye`), the name used for gating (`antigen`) and its `type`:

- `scatter`: forward and side scatter, shown on linear axes;
- `time`;
- `lineage` and `activation`: fluorescence channels, shown on logicle axes.
  Medians are reported for both.

`create.panel.file()` drafts a panel from an FCS file.

The **experiment file** (`fcs_experiment_st1.csv`) lists the FCS files, a
sample name for each, and `gate.calculation`: `TRUE` for the samples whose
events are pooled to train the gates. `create.experiment.file()` drafts it
from a metadata table and a folder of FCS files.

The **parameters** (`get.autogating.param()`) name these files and the
cytometer, whose defaults set the display transforms and figure ranges.
Optional files add a compensation (spillover) matrix for conventional data
and per-channel transforms (`transformation.filename`, Gating-ML or FlowJo
biex columns, keyed by dye).

```{r}
library( AutoGating )

st1.dir <- "scripts/ST1"
ap <- get.autogating.param(
    cytometer                 = "symphony",
    data.dir                  = "path/to/st1_fcs",
    panel.filename            = file.path( st1.dir, "fcs_panel_st1.csv" ),
    experiment.filename       = file.path( st1.dir, "fcs_experiment_st1.csv" ),
    compensation.filename     = file.path( st1.dir, "fcs_compensation_st1.csv" ),
    transformation.filename   = file.path( st1.dir, "fcs_transformation_st1.csv" ),
    population.gates.filename = file.path( st1.dir, "fcs_population_gates_st1.r" ),
    activation.gates.filename = file.path( st1.dir, "fcs_activation_gates_st1.r" ),
    statistics.dir            = "st1_output/statistics",
    figure.dir                = "st1_output/figures",
    worker.n                  = 4L
)
```

## Reading the data

`setup.autogating()` reads each FCS file (`AutoSpectral::readFCS`), keeps the
panel channels, applies the compensation, and puts every channel on the
display scale used for gating: 0 to 1, with 1 the top of the instrument range.
Fluorescence channels use the logicle transform (linear around zero, log for
bright events), scatter channels a linear one. Thresholds and polygons are
stored on this scale, the same scale Honeychrome and FlowKit use.

```{r}
fcs.setup <- setup.autogating( ap )
```

## Gates

Each gate has a type, a parent population and an algorithm:

- **singlets**: a band around the line of FSC-H against FSC-A; doublets fall
  below it. The band is 3 robust standard deviations wide (`width.sd`).
- **free**: "cells" draws a rectangle on FSC and SSC from the debris cut up
  to where the cells' density fades; "all" is the outline of every event.
- **1dsep**: one threshold on one channel, giving the populations below and
  above it. It can be shown against a second channel.
- **2dsep**: a threshold on each of two channels, giving four quadrants;
  quadrants can be joined into one population (three quadrants make an L).
- **replicate**: the same gate as another one, applied to a different parent.

Thresholds come from the data of the parent population:

- **mixture**: fits two bell curves (negative and positive) and puts the
  threshold where they cross. Best when both populations are present.
- **tail**: puts the threshold just above the negative population, so that
  only a set small fraction (0.0001) of a symmetric negative would be called
  positive. Best for a rare or dim positive population.
- **kde_min**: the lowest point of the density between the two peaks.
- **otsu**: the cut that best separates the events into two groups.
- **replicate**: copies another gate's threshold on the same channel, or
  calculates it on a reference population (for example the same marker on
  all CD4 T cells, then used on each CD4 subset).

The ST1 gates are R lists in the earlier AutoGating format;
`define.gates()` converts them (`convert.gate.definitions()`) and trains
every gate on the pooled training events (`ap$events.per.sample`, 50,000 per
training sample). It also draws each gate on the training events in
`figures/training`.

```{r}
model <- define.gates( fcs.setup, ap )
write.agmodel( model, "st1_output/st1.agmodel", fcs.setup$fcs.panel )
```

A model saved from Honeychrome, or by `write.agmodel()`, is used instead of
the gate lists with `model.filename`. A FlowJo workspace is imported with
`import.flowjo.workspace()`; its drawn gates can then be turned into
calculated gates with `convert.imported.gates()`.

## Editing in the app

`autogating.app()` opens the model in a browser: the gate hierarchy with each
population's share of its parent, the figure of each gate, and an editor for
its parent, channels, populations, algorithm and settings. Clicking a figure
sets a manual threshold. Transforms can be changed with a live preview.
Every change is recalculated at once and can be undone.

```{r}
edited <- autogating.app( fcs.setup, ap, model )
model <- edited$model
```

## Gating every sample

`run.autogating()` applies the model to each sample on its own (in parallel
with `worker.n > 1`) and writes three tables to `statistics.dir`: the count
and fraction of every population in every sample, the median of every
fluorescence channel in every population, and the status of every gate in
every sample (where its boundary came from, how far it moved, and any flag).

```{r}
gating <- run.autogating( fcs.setup, model, ap )
subset( gating$status, !is.na( flag ) )
```

With `figure.samples = TRUE` in the parameters, every gate is also drawn on
every sample.

## Comparing groups

`differential.statistics()` compares groups of samples. Each population's
frequency is tested as the log odds of an event being in the population
rather than elsewhere in its parent: this treats a change from 1% to 2% and
from 49% to 66% alike (both double the odds) and keeps rare populations from
being swamped by common ones. Marker medians are compared on the display
scale. Both use limma's moderated t-tests, which borrow strength across
populations, with an optional pairing (the same individual in several
groups) and covariates. p-values are adjusted for the number of tests
(Benjamini-Hochberg).

```{r}
samples <- data.frame( sample = gating$population.table$sample, stringsAsFactors = FALSE )
samples <- unique( samples )
samples$group <- c( "control", "treated" )[ 1 + ( seq_len( nrow( samples ) ) > 12 ) ]

stats <- differential.statistics( gating, samples, group.column = "group",
                                  output.dir = "st1_output/differential" )
head( stats$frequencies[ stats$frequencies$significant, ] )
```

The output folder holds the test tables, the values per sample, volcano
plots, maps of the significant differences and per-sample plots by group.
